## TL;DR

Added coverage for the release email’s real provider wiring from `deliverCutReleaseEmail` through `sendEmail` and into a local HTTP endpoint. The test checks that the sender, authorization header, JSON payload, and per-recipient delivery behavior match the Resend contract. It uses the existing fake test key and `.test` addresses; the network request is redirected to loopback, so no real mail can be sent.

## Work and rationale

The task targeted a gap between two existing test layers. Release email tests already verified the delivery loop by injecting a fake `fetch`, while `sendEmail` owned the Resend URL, authorization header, `From` formatting, JSON body, and one-recipient request shape. A regression in those shared wiring details could therefore pass the release tests.

The new test lives beside the existing release email tests in `src/ui-app/tests/release-email.test.ts`. It starts an HTTP server bound only to `127.0.0.1` on an ephemeral port, captures each request’s headers and parsed JSON body, and responds with a successful provider-shaped response. Its injected fetch adapter asserts that the production code requested `https://api.resend.com/emails`, then forwards the request options to the local server URL. This preserves the production `sendEmail` implementation and exercises the actual request construction while avoiding external network traffic.

The test invokes `deliverCutReleaseEmail` with the normal release fixture and configured fake Resend credentials. It verifies the final sent record, accepted recipient list, request count, bearer authorization value, sender header, recipient array, subject, HTML, and text fields. Comparing the payload for each recipient ensures the implementation sends one separately addressed message per recipient rather than a single multi-recipient message. The server is closed in a `finally` block so failures in assertions do not leave a listener behind.

No production code changes were necessary: the existing seams (`ReleaseEmailDeps.fetchImpl`) are enough to route the shared provider request locally without changing the public endpoint or adding dependencies. The test uses the existing `FAKE_KEY`, `FAKE_FROM`, and `.test` recipient addresses, which are explicitly non-live values.

## Approaches tried

The branch already contained the implementation from its previous engineer checkpoint when this session resumed, so I inspected the task specification, the test setup, the test body, and the production send path before altering anything. The local endpoint adapter proved to be the right seam: mocking `sendEmail` would skip the request construction under test, while globally replacing `fetch` could obscure whether the production Resend URL was still used. Forwarding only requests to the expected Resend URL keeps that assertion explicit and sends the actual request options to loopback.

I ran `repoos check --fix`; its full check plan completed successfully. I then ran the required `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check`, which built the branch, ran the changed and always-run test files, completed the UI smoke test and rendered contrast audit, and reported “All checks passed.” The changed-path suite included the new local endpoint test, which passed.

## Challenges and blockers

This is a tests-only change, so there is no UI behavior to capture. The test’s loopback setup must close reliably; cleanup is protected by `finally`. The prior run’s activity recorded that the new test passed remotely but formatting stopped later local gates. This session completed both the formatter-enabled full check and the required scoped check successfully. The worktree has no source changes pending beyond the task branch checkpoint; generated build output remains local.

## Key learnings

A small injected-fetch adapter can test provider wiring end to end without making a live provider call: assert the production URL, preserve its headers/body/signal, and forward the options to a local HTTP server. That gives concrete coverage of HTTP serialization and headers while keeping the release delivery test close to the real application path. Keeping test credentials in a named fake constant and using reserved `.test` addresses makes the no-real-mail property visible in the fixture itself.
